doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: International House and the Band Box in Menlo Park
summary: Working for Morrie Waxman in uniform, then in the postwar quartet with Collette, Ernie Royal and Jimmy Shorter.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: So it was a wonderful experience. And when Buddy Collette and Ernie, eventually they went back to Los Angeles. See after the war I got a job in late ’45, just as I was getting out the service, I got a job at the Band Box in Menlo Park working for Morrie Waxman. Now Morrie had had a club in San Francisco during the war called the International House. It was located on Columbus just across from the Barbary Coast — what was called the Barbary Coast, that was Pacific Avenue. And it was down in the basement, sawdust on the floor, big barrels for tables, small barrels for chairs. And they had a big bandstand. And I was in uniform and I worked there for him. And I used to do the extended drum solos and everything, and so I must have worked for him for six months. And we weren’t supposed to you know, because the union had an agreement with the Twelfth Naval District that the union musicians wouldn’t compete with the local musicians. But there weren’t enough local musicians to fill all these jobs. Because you had — if you look in our Chronicle now you see all these little clubs. Well that’s what we had during the war. Every little spot had something. Piano, piano and bass, piano drums guitar. Every little spot, all the North Beach, Chinatown, down Market Street, the Barbary Coast was wall to wall on each side of the street, clubs — bars and clubs. So I got that job down there playing, and it was good for me because I had the chance to work out these extended drum solos which later, during my course at St. Mary’s College, because what I’d do you could hitchhike then, you didn’t have to worry about transportation. So I’d hitchhike over to the International House and do my set, we played nine till two, then I’d hitchhike home, then I’d get up in the morning and we’d go out to St. Mary’s and we’d practice all day and do our duties, our musical duties all day. So that was quite a period. Anyhow Morrie Waxman, after the war he moved down, he went down the peninsula and opened up this spot. And he hired us. We worked there for a year. Had Buddy Collette and Ernie Royal and as I say Jimmy Shorter. So that job, Buddy Colette was the first one back to Los Angeles and I got Curtis Lowe to play tenor to take his place. Then after a year, so Curtis, he must have come in, Buddy was there for most of the engagement. I think maybe the last two months Curtis played. And then I got Jimmy Shorter so he left. Jimmy Shorter, he was a railway mail clerk back in Washington, D.C. He was one of the first that they had. So he had taken a military leave so he said well it’s time for me to go back. So I got Ali Mishaw, who had been the drummer for Scatman.

Scatman Crothers. An excellent pianist. So I got him, and so that association lasted — let’s see we played, as I said Buddy was the first one to leave and then Jimmy Shorter, he went back to Washington, D.C., Buddy went back to Los Angeles, so that was Ernie and Curtis and Ali and I. And we got a job, we left there and we got a job at the Slim Jenkins in Oakland. He was quite the guy. The place was in West Oakland at that time. And it was a cabaret, I mean first class.
